title: Unified Customer Hub
subtitle: Turning three disconnected fintech products into one platform — and 420K+ monthly users

meta.label: Role
meta.value: Lead Designer — vision to shipped product

value: Best Egg offered personal loans, credit cards, and financial-health tools. On paper, one brand. In reality, three products that shared a logo and a color — and almost nothing else.

The business wanted to grow through cross-sell: turn a loan customer into a card customer, nudge a card user to watch their credit score. But the products never spoke to each other, and neither did the experiences. Every new launch shipped as its own island, quietly eroding cohesion and every cross-sell opportunity with it.
The obvious problem was fragmentation. The real one was quieter: no one owned the word "unified."
Each product line had its own PM, its own KPIs, its own roadmap. Everyone agreed unification mattered — then nothing moved. The vision floated, and no one was there to catch it.
That vacuum, I decided, was exactly where design should step in. Only design could take an abstract word and turn it into something everyone could point at.

blocks.label: Framing question
blocks.value: How might we unify loans, cards, and financial health into one trusted platform — without disrupting core workflows or overloading a legacy stack?

blocks.label: Stakeholder tension map — three product lines, three KPI sets, and an unowned "Unified?" in the middle

value: Instead of pitching a deck, I spent two weeks building a clickable, high-fidelity prototype — a real flow: pay off a loan, jump to your credit score, land on a cross-sell entry point, seamlessly.
In the review, I didn't argue we should unify. I let stakeholders click it themselves.

blocks.label: Prototype walkthrough — loan → credit score → cross-sell

blocks.value: Oh — so THAT's what cross-sell looks like.
The vision finally had a shape. And I became the de-facto driver of a project that never had an owner.

value: Engineering pushed back hard. Credit Card ran on a third-party platform. Migrating it in-house meant 6+ months and a real risk of breaking live servicing flows. The vision was beautiful — and, right now, unbuildable.
I didn't debate feasibility. I mapped complexity with them.

In a working session with Engineering and PM, I enumerated every account state — single-product, loan + card, card + financial health, past-due, pending activation, missing data — into one account-state reference table.
Laid out, it made something obvious: only a handful of high-frequency shared surfaces were truly interconnected. Everything else was account-specific and didn't need to move at once.

The call: keep Credit Card on the third-party platform for now. Focus in-house effort on the highest-impact surfaces — unified dashboard, Loan, Financial Health. Stitch the card in through an integration layer. Bring it home later, once the platform proved its value.
The hard part: this plan was imperfect for everyone. So I told three stories for one decision.

blocks.value: Same decision, three narratives. That's what moving a project forward really means — not making everyone love the same reason, but letting everyone nod from the angle they care about.

items.label: To Engineering
items.title: Feasible and safe
items.desc: This avoids the riskiest migration and keeps you on schedule.

items.label: To business & leadership
items.title: Results first
items.desc: The surfaces we ship first are exactly where cross-sell converts. We'll see data fastest.

items.label: To design
items.title: The vision, protected
items.desc: Keeping card third-party protects the vision. We validate the platform first, then earn the right to bring it home.

blocks.value: Three products × ownership combinations × account states = a combinatorial explosion. Miss one state, and a user hits a blank page. So I didn't draw every screen — I built systems.

items.title: Customer Hub
items.desc: A centralized dashboard unifying Financial Health, Personal Loan, and Credit Card data into a single, clear view of a customer's financial status.

items.title: Personal Loan
items.desc: A dedicated space to view payment history, access statements, and make payments with ease.

items.title: Financial Health
items.desc: Credit scores, score factors, alerts, simulations, and access to detailed credit reports.

blocks.title: A messaging framework, not one-off designs

value: With Marketing and a researcher, I tested cross-sell placements on UserTesting. The finding was sharp: banners and in-feature messaging performed best with minimal annoyance; modals felt intrusive and belonged only to critical alerts.

I didn't spend the insight and move on — I codified it into a reusable "message urgency ↔ placement" mapping: what level of message, in which placement, with what motion intensity. Every product line and every engineer could place messages by rule, instead of coming back to ask me — turning a one-off design into a self-serve system.

blocks.value: Key user testing insights: we tested 20 message-placement combinations across 527 users. Banners and in-feature messaging won on engagement and sentiment; modals felt intrusive and were reserved for critical alerts.

blocks.title: Designing for products that didn't exist yet

value: Best Egg keeps launching products. If each spun up its own flow, we'd slide right back into fragmentation. So the Best Egg Design System — 2,000+ modular components — was built to be pluggable: navigation, shared modules, and the messaging framework all reserved insertion points for future products.

I wasn't delivering a platform. I was delivering a platform that could grow new products — the same extensibility that later made room for smarter, AI-driven personalization. An extensible architecture is the prerequisite for embracing whatever ships next.

blocks.label: Best Egg Design System — 2,000+ modular components

blocks.value: Launched August 2022. The gains showed up immediately and kept compounding. In the first week, credit score activation post-login rose 94% and Financial Health daily active users more than doubled — proof the unified entry point was doing exactly what it was designed to do: get customers to the products that mattered before they even asked.

blocks.label: Launch announcement and early-results readout to the team

blocks.value: On the revenue side, second-loan eligibility climbed to 42% (vs. 35% on the legacy servicing site) with a 50% acceptance rate, and the leads chart told the same story more slowly: the Hub's share of second-loan leads crept up week over week until, by mid-August, it had overtaken the legacy channel outright.
